summary: Forest Fire Lookout Association lists a Tyler County tower named Emilee as gone; the name matches a former community, but no source found describes the tower's build, staff or site today.

facts.status_note: Listed as Tower Gone by the Forest Fire Lookout Association; no later status found

evidence.supports: listed as Tower Gone in Tyler County at 30.83852, -94.27811
former community ten miles northeast of present Woodville
evidence.quote: Emilee (Emille) was ten miles northeast of the site of present Woodville in eastern Tyler County.

evidence.supports: named for Emilee McClendon, wife of John B. McClendon
evidence.quote: The community was named for Emilee McClendon, the wife of John B. McClendon, an early settler.
The Emilee post office functioned from 1904 to 1946.

evidence.supports: population fifty by 1900 and fifty in 1948 count
evidence.quote: By 1900 the population had fallen to fifty, the same figure cited in 1948 in the community's last available population count.

evidence.supports: community disappeared; still on some maps as Emille
evidence.quote: After that the community disappeared, although it appeared on some maps (as Emille).

sources.title: Emilee, TX
sources.publisher: Handbook of Texas Online, Texas State Historical Association

notes_for_editor: The only lookout-specific source is the undated Forest Fire Lookout Association list, which gives a name, coordinates, type and Tower Gone status. Nothing read gives a build date, design, height, staffing, fire record or the reason it came down. The name matches the former community of Emilee (TSHA), but no source links the tower to the town, so the story does not say the tower was named for it. Texas Escapes also has a page on Emilee; its line-broken text was not quoted. The Portal to Texas History searches for Emilee lookout and Emilee fire tower returned nothing. Lookout histories by Bob Bowman (Texas Escapes) and the book Fire in the Piney Woods (Cavallerano) are the likely places to look for a build date. No photos added.
